title: Globalization & Business Ethics Adventure 1: MNCs & Globalization
welcome_lead: Today you'll explore multinational corporations and the forces of globalization.
meta_desc: Business Management: MNCs, drivers of globalization, costs and benefits to host countries.
final_note: You assessed the costs and benefits of MNCs for host and home countries.

concepts.def: Firm with operations in multiple countries
Investment by firm in foreign assets
Internal prices to shift profit to low-tax

walkthroughs.body_html:
An MNC produces or sells in two or more countries.

Drivers of growth: cheaper labour, larger markets, escaping tariffs, accessing raw materials, tax planning.

Examples: Apple (US HQ, China assembly), Toyota (Japan, plants worldwide), Unilever (UK/NL, 190 countries).

FDI brings jobs, tax revenue, technology transfer, exports, and supplier industries.

It can break a low-income trap by injecting capital and skills, raising productivity (the East Asian model).

Costs: profit repatriation, environmental damage, exploitation of weak labour laws, undermining local firms, cultural homogenisation, transfer pricing to dodge tax.

Host governments respond with FDI rules, local content quotas and minimum standards.

options: Dumping
Transfer pricing
Tariff arbitrage
Surge pricing

mcqs.q: When can a laissez-faire leadership style be effective?
options: Stakeholders are managers and shareholders are workers.
Laissez-faire leadership means the leader doesn't care about the business.
Laissez-faire leadership is illegal under employment law.
When employees are highly skilled, self-motivated and need autonomy — common in creative or expert teams. It can fail with inexperienced staff or in crises requiring direction.

mcqs.q: Which sector does manufacturing belong to?
options: Laissez-faire leadership is illegal under employment law.
The secondary sector — which transforms raw materials from the primary sector (farming, mining) into finished goods.
Manufacturing is in the primary sector because it makes things.
Manufacturing is in the tertiary sector along with services.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a stakeholder and a shareholder?
options: A shareholder owns shares in the company; a stakeholder is anyone affected by or with interest in the business — employees, customers, suppliers, community, plus shareholders.
Laissez-faire leadership is illegal under employment law.
Stakeholders are managers and shareholders are workers.
Stakeholders and shareholders are different spellings of the same word.
